title: Notation, the clock and slow games

bank.prompt: White's first move is written 1.d4. Tap the square the pawn lands on.
bank.reason: No capital letter means a pawn move, and what is left is the square it goes to.

bank.prompt: White plays Nc3. A capital N means knight. Tap the square the knight lands on.
bank.reason: The letter names the piece, the rest names the square it arrives on.

bank.prompt: White plays Bb5. Tap the square the bishop lands on.
bank.reason: B is the bishop and b5 is where it goes. Only the bishop on f1 can get there.

bank.prompt: White plays exd5. Tap the square the capturing pawn lands on.
bank.reason: The small e says which pawn is capturing. The square at the end is always where it lands.

bank.prompt: Castling on the queen's side is written O-O-O. Tap the square the white king finishes on.
bank.reason: The king always travels two squares when it castles, so e1 becomes c1.

bank.prompt: White castles queenside, written O-O-O. Tap the square the white rook finishes on.
bank.reason: The rook jumps over the king and lands beside it on d1.

bank.prompt: Both white rooks can reach e1, and the move played is written Rfe1. Tap the square that rook came from.
bank.reason: When two identical pieces can reach one square, the file the mover started on is added.

bank.prompt: A written move ends with a + sign. What is it telling you?
options: The move captures something.
The move gives check.
The move ends the game.
bank.reason: A plus means check. Mate gets its own mark, the hash.

bank.prompt: A written move ends with a # sign. What is it telling you?
options: It is check, and the game carries on.
It is mate, and the game is over there.
A pawn promoted on that square.
bank.reason: The hash is the last thing written in a game, because nothing follows mate.

bank.prompt: In the written move Bxc6, what is the x telling you?
options: The bishop takes whatever is standing on c6.
The bishop is defended once it reaches c6.
The bishop started on the c-file.
bank.reason: An x always means a capture, and the square after it is where the capture happens.

bank.prompt: Why does the written move e4 have no capital letter in front of it?
options: It is a king move, and the king is understood.
It is a pawn move, and pawns have no letter of their own.
The letter is left off when the move is not a capture.
bank.reason: Every other piece has a letter. A bare square is how a pawn move is written.

bank.prompt: Black to move. The move written here is Qh4#. Read it, then play it on the board.

wrong.Qg5: That is not the square the move names. Qh4 means the queen lands on h4.

bank.reason: Q is the queen, h4 is the square, and # says the game ends there. Nothing covers h4 or blocks the diagonal.

bank.prompt: White to move. The move written here is Rxd8#. Read it, then play it on the board.

wrong.Rd4: You have read the letter and ignored the square. Rxd8 takes on d8.

bank.reason: R is the rook, x is the capture, d8 is the square, and # says it is mate.

bank.prompt: Play these moves exactly as they are written: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3. Black's replies are played for you.
bank.reason: Three moves each, in the order they were played, written the way every chess book writes them.

bank.prompt: White plays Nxe5. Tap the square the knight lands on.
bank.reason: N is the knight, x is the capture, and e5 is the square it arrives on.

bank.prompt: The pawn on d5 looks free and the rook can take it. Is the rook safe there?
reasons: Yes. Nothing black can reach d5.
No. The king on g8 takes it back.
No. The knight on c7 takes it back.
bank.reason: Nc7 covers d5. The ten seconds it takes to notice save a whole rook.

bank.prompt: The same capture on a different board. The rook takes on d5. Is it safe there?
reasons: No. The king on g8 takes it back.
No. The pawn on e6 takes it back.
Yes. Nothing black defends d5.
bank.reason: There is no pawn on e6 and the king is three squares away. Sometimes the check says yes, and it costs the same either way.

bank.prompt: The rook takes the pawn on e5. Is it safe there?
reasons: Yes. Nothing defends e5.
No. The pawn on f6 takes it back.
No. The king on g8 takes it back.
bank.reason: A pawn defender is the one the eye skips, which is exactly why you look twice before you commit.

bank.prompt: The rook takes the knight on d5. Is it safe there?
reasons: Yes. Nothing black reaches d5.
No. The king on g8 takes it back.
No. The bishop on a2 takes it back.
bank.reason: The bishop on a2 looks along a2-b3-c4-d5. A defender from the far corner is worth a second look.

bank.prompt: The rook takes on e5, and there is a black rook on d7. Is the white rook safe on e5?
reasons: No. The rook on d7 takes it back.
Yes. The rook on d7 is on the wrong file.
No. The pawn on f6 takes it back.
bank.reason: The rook on d7 is the frightening piece and the pawn on f6 is the one that takes. Look at everything, not at the biggest thing.

bank.prompt: The rook takes the knight on e4. Is it safe there?
reasons: No. The pawn on f7 takes it back.
Yes. Nothing black defends e4.
No. The king on g8 takes it back.
bank.reason: A pawn on f7 captures to e6 or g6, and the king is far away. This knight really is free.

bank.prompt: Your rook is attacked and there is plenty of time left. Do not move it away. Look along the file first.

wrong.Rb1: Running saved the rook and missed mate in one. The rook was attacked, and that is exactly what made you hurry.

bank.reason: Rxa8 takes the rook and mates on the eighth rank at the same time. Running was the fast answer and the wrong one.

bank.prompt: Your rook is attacked by the queen. Do not run. Look up the file first.

wrong.Rb1: The rook is safe and the queen is still standing. Rxd4 was there the whole time.

bank.reason: The queen on d4 is undefended and on your rook's file. Being attacked is what makes people move before they look.

bank.prompt: You have twelve minutes left in a thirty-minute game and you see a capture straight away. What comes next?
options: Play it now, while you can still see it.
Work out what your opponent plays in reply, then decide.
Play something safer instead, to save thinking time.
bank.reason: The first move you see is a candidate. Checking the reply is the cheapest ten seconds in chess.

bank.prompt: Your opponent has just played a move that attacks your queen. What does a strong player do first?
options: Move the queen at once to the nearest safe square.
Look at what that move stopped defending.
Offer a draw before anything worse happens.
bank.reason: Every move that creates a threat also leaves something behind. Fear is what stops people looking.

bank.prompt: You finish a slow game with eighteen of your thirty minutes unused. What does that tell you?
options: You should ask for a shorter time control next game.
You played efficiently and should carry on doing it.
You did not use the time you were given to check your moves.
bank.reason: Time left over at the end is worth nothing. Spend it on the moves that decide things, and keep enough back not to flag.

bank.prompt: Your game review lists an Inaccuracy on move 9 and a Blunder on move 31. Which do you study first?
options: Move 31, because it is the one you still remember.
Move 31. The bigger the error, the bigger the lesson.
Move 9. Everything after it was played in a position that was already worse.
bank.reason: The earliest error decided what kind of game the rest of it was. Fix that and the later one often never arises.

bank.prompt: The review labels one of your moves a Miss. What has it found?
options: A good chance you had and did not take.
A move that gave away material outright.
A move that came straight out of the opening book.
bank.reason: A Miss is a chance that was there. It is the label most worth going back to, because the chance will come again.

bank.prompt: The review labels one of your moves Book. What does that mean?
options: It is a known opening move, so it was not your own decision yet.
It is a move the engine has never seen before.
It is the strongest move played in the whole game.
bank.reason: Book moves are not marked good or bad. The review tells you the move at which your game left the book, and that is where your own choices start.

bank.prompt: The review marks the moves and hands the positions back. What is the one job it cannot do for you?
options: Saying out loud what you missed, in words you will remember.
Deciding which of your moves were mistakes.
Showing you the position as it stood before your move.
bank.reason: Naming the thing you missed is what makes you see it next time, and it is the only part of the review that is your work.

bank.prompt: A review ends with a short drill built out of your own errors. What is it for?
options: Replaying the moves you did not have time to play.
Raising your puzzle rating as quickly as possible.
Practising the exact things you got wrong in that game.
bank.reason: The drill comes from your error log, not from a general pile of puzzles. A clean game ends with no drill rather than a padded one.

bank.prompt: The review hands this position back as a key moment. Your bishop is attacked and in the game you moved it away. Find what you had.

wrong.Bc3: The bishop is still on her diagonal, so Qxc3 just takes it. Bxe5 was there the whole time.

bank.reason: The queen on e5 stands on the bishop's own diagonal with nothing defending her. The threat to the bishop is what made the move look urgent.

bank.prompt: Another key moment from the same game. The review says you had better here. Find it.

wrong.Rd2: Nothing was attacking the rook. Rxd4 wins the bishop for nothing.

bank.reason: The rook and the bishop stand on the same file with nothing between them and nothing defending d4.

bank.prompt: This is the move the review marked. The rook takes the knight on d5. Was it safe?
reasons: Yes. Nothing defends the knight on d5.
No. The king on e8 takes it back.
No. The pawn on c6 takes it back.
bank.reason: cxd5 wins a rook for a knight. The review will keep handing this back until you start looking at pawns.

bank.prompt: The same capture with the c-pawn gone. The rook takes on d5. Was it safe?
reasons: Yes. Nothing black reaches d5.
No. The pawn on c6 takes it back.
No. The king on e8 takes it back.
bank.reason: One pawn is the whole difference between a winning move and a losing one, which is why the review goes square by square.

bank.prompt: A position from your own game, White to move. Tap every white piece Black could take for nothing.
bank.reason: The bishop on e5 rakes both diagonals, hitting a1 one way and h2 the other, and the pawn on a6 takes the knight on b5. Nothing white defends any of the three.

bank.prompt: The review shows the position before your move Rd4 and says there was mate in one. Tap the square the rook should have gone to.
bank.reason: Rxd8 is mate on the eighth rank. A key moment hands the position back so you can find it yourself.
